P01.explanation: The young men crossed into the neighboring parish, cut down its maypole, fought off the neighbors who tried to stop them, and burned the pole at home, so the walk was a "raid": a foray to seize something from rivals by force. "Roundup" fails because they ran home past the grazing ponies and brought back only the pole. "Pilgrimage" fails because what they went to was the neighbors' green, and what they did there was cut down and carry off the neighbors' pole, not honor a place. "Pageant" fails because, despite the soot on their faces, the fight was real: the neighbors ran out to stop them, and the pole was really taken and burned.

P02.explanation: "Cemetery" fits: young voles settle in the strip, and owls hunting from the poles kill more than half of them within a month, so the strip is where the voles die. "Corridor" fails because the voles stop within a few hundred yards of where they entered and are killed there within weeks, so none passes along the strip toward the other forest. "Cage" fails because voles can wander back to the forest edge, so the strip does not hold them in. "Cafeteria" fails because, for all its seed, the young voles move into the strip to live after being pushed out of the forest edges; they do not come to eat and go home.

P03.explanation: "Groomed" fits: the sheep keep the whole slope cropped to an even, inch-high turf where low flowers bloom, while the slope they cannot reach has run to brambles and tussocks, so the flock keeps its hillside trimmed and tidy. "Denuded" fails because the turf is continuous; the slope is cropped short, not stripped bare. "Fertilized" fails because the soil tests no richer than the ungrazed slope's. "Furrowed" fails because the sheep wander in every direction and have worn no paths.

P04.explanation: Each stretch of the river held stones of nearly one size, oven-sized boulders at the cliffs, cobbles four miles down, gravel at the sea, so the river had separated them by size along its course: it had "sorted" them. "Stacked" means set one on another, but painted stones moved a mile downstream with each flood and lay wherever they stopped. "Stained" means given a color from outside, but a cracked stone showed the same shade inside as out. "Sanded" means worn down by grit, but even at the sea broken pebbles still fit back together edge to edge, so their edges had lost nothing.

P05.explanation: The marsh's water leaves on sunny afternoons with half again as much oxygen as the bay, and fish gather at its mouth exactly when the bay's deep water runs short of oxygen, so the marsh is the bay's "lung," its source of oxygen. "Kitchen" fails because the fish come only in late summer and on the afternoon ebbs, the times when the bay lacks oxygen and the marsh's water is richest in it, so they are drawn by the oxygen rather than by food the marsh sends out. "Kidney" fails because the water left carrying all the creek's fertilizer nitrate. "Net" fails because it ran out as brown with mud as it came in.

P06.explanation: The miller lined both banks with cut stone for a quarter mile, so the once wandering stream ran straight between them: the mill "walled" the stream. "Siphoned" means drew water away, but the whole stream ran past the wheel. "Stilled" means calmed the current, but the stone banks sped the stream into a quick current that turned the wheel. "Soured" means fouled the water, but trout below the mill were as many as above it.

P07.explanation: As it melted the glacier spread forty feet of clay, sand and stones evenly from wall to wall, and every well passes through that layer before reaching rock, so the glacier "mantled" the valley floor, covering it entirely. "Littered" fails because the stones are mixed through a continuous layer whose surface is smooth enough to plow, not strewn separately across the ground. "Milled" fails because the granite under the layer still has its crumbling crust from before the ice, which a grinding glacier would have scraped away first. "Incised" fails because the river has cut no more than ten feet into the layer and never reaches the floor beneath.

P08.explanation: "Hearth" fits: the bricks on the wall's sunny face hold heat into the night, and the peaches trained against them set fruit in springs when frost kills the blossom everywhere else, so the wall is the orchard's source of warmth. "Fence" fails because the wall runs along one edge only and is open at both ends, so it closes nothing in or out. "Dike" fails because the river runs past the orchard's southern edge while the wall stands on its northern edge, with the trees between them, so the wall cannot hold the river off the orchard. "Firebreak" fails because the village lies across the river, and when it burned, the fire stopped at the water; it never came near the wall on the orchard's far side.

P09.explanation: Miners left watches, pistols and a fiddle in the safe as security for credit, redeemed them when they struck pay dirt, and lost them to sale each fall if they did not, so the store was the camp's "pawnshop": a lender against pledged goods. "Repository" fails because the goods were not simply kept for their owners; they secured debts, and the unredeemed ones were sold. "Parlor" fails because the merchant banked the stove and barred the door at sundown, so no one gathered there in the evenings. "Pharmacy" fails because the bottles held whiskey.

P10.explanation: Paths from both neighborhoods cross the park to a footbridge and a train station, and thirty thousand people a day walk them at rush hour without lingering, so the park is the district's "junction," where its routes meet on the way somewhere else. "Magnet" fails because the walkers are mostly local residents headed for the train, not people drawn in from elsewhere to spend time there. "Mixer" fails because people spend only the ten minutes the walk takes and the benches stand empty, so the park is crossed rather than used as a place where the two neighborhoods' residents spend time together. "Muffler" fails because the lawns slope open to the highway, leaving nothing to absorb its noise.

P11.explanation: "Gallery" fits: the paintings were hung on lit walls and townspeople came down every week to walk past them, so the mine was where the museum showed its collection. "Depository" fails because the paintings were not packed away out of reach; they hung uncrated and were seen by crowds every Sunday, which is display, not safekeeping. "Hospital" fails because the paintings stayed unchanged; nothing was repaired. "Dump" fails because every painting went back up to the new building.

P12.explanation: Planks that look sound from outside crumble into a lace of pencil-wide tunnels, so the sea and its creatures had "mined" the ship, boring through it from within while leaving its outside shape. "Mummified" fails because a mummified hull keeps its substance, and these planks fell apart at a touch; only the outward shape survived. "Interred" fails because the hull stood upright on the open bottom, not buried. "Jostled" fails because the hull still stood upright with its cargo in the hold, where it had settled.

P13.explanation: "Churned" fits: the turbines run in afternoon bursts, so every day the river surges four feet in an hour and then drops away, and the gravel bars keep shifting, which means the dam keeps stirring the river up. "Bled" fails because the water that drops away at night comes back in a four-foot rise each afternoon, so the dam is holding back and releasing the river's water, not taking it away. "Chilled" fails because the water comes from just beneath the reservoir's sunlit surface, and bass, which need warm water, still spawn just below the dam. "Clogged" fails because gravel bars that shift week to week never sit still long enough for silt and plants to choke the channel.

P14.explanation: "Deforested" fits: the aspens that once covered both slopes for two hundred yards are now only gnawed stumps, so the beavers have cleared their valley of trees. "Flooded" fails because their dams wash out each spring and the creek runs in the same shallow bed as the one next door, so no water stands on the valley. "Dredged" fails because that bed is still shallow and stony, the same as in the valley without beavers. "Greened" fails because in dry summers the valley turns just as brown as its neighbor.

P15.explanation: The lines list ingredients and stages in order, barley sprouted and then crushed, dates, water, and a three-day wait, with a second column doubling every amount, under the brewer's seal and worn by handling, so the tablet is the brewer's "recipe": quantities and steps for a brew in two batch sizes. "Receipt" fails because the doubled column scales one set of quantities, which a record of goods actually handed over would have no reason to do, and the seal is the brewer's own. "Payroll" fails because no line names a person. "Roadmap" fails because the three days fall between stages of the same barley, sprouted and then crushed, in one brewery, not between places on a route.

P16.explanation: Corals and sponges have grown out along every beam of the hull while the bare sand around it holds almost none, so the hull is a framework that living things grow along: a "trellis." A "tomb" holds the dead, but all thirty of the crew rowed ashore. A "strongbox" keeps valuables secure, but the hull held only coal, left where it fell. A "tripwire" is a hidden hazard that catches the unwary, but the island's ferries pass over the wreck twice a day.

P17.explanation: The drought shrank the soil from the roots, and in the next gales a fifth of the pines went down with their roots torn out, so the dry years brought the trees down: they "toppled" the forest. "Winnowed" means removed the weak and left the strong, but the trees that fell were mostly the tallest and soundest on the ridges. "Scorched" means burned or browned, but the pines kept green needles through every dry summer. "Sapped" means drained of strength, but the standing pines grew rings as wide as before the drought.

P18.explanation: "Garnered" fits: at the end of the season the workers collected the aphids' eggs, kept them heaped underground through the winter, and the next year's aphids came out of that store, so the ants gathered the aphids in and laid them up like a harvest. "Herded" fails because all summer the ants never moved aphids even off wilting shoots, and in spring the young climbed out on their own; the only carrying was eggs going into storage, not animals being driven to pasture. "Devoured" fails because the eggs taken underground were not eaten: they hatched in spring and the young left alive. "Drugged" fails because aphids walked as fast on ant-crossed leaves as on clean ones.

P19.explanation: The editors met weekly with the war ministry, ran its recruiting appeals free, printed its casualty lists and urged readers to enlist in their own columns, so the government "mobilized" the press, enlisting it in the war effort. "Muzzled" fails because no censor read the pages, and the peace appeals were dropped by the editors themselves, who were now writing for the war, so the press was recruited rather than silenced. "Nationalized" fails because the papers stayed in private hands. "Impoverished" fails because their sales climbed.

P20.explanation: The wolves' kills were mostly old cows with worn teeth and elk lame from hoof rot, and with fewer mouths competing for winter grass more calves lived to spring, so old animals were replaced by young while the count held: the wolves "rejuvenated" the herd. "Reduced" fails because the extra calves held the count near 900. "Redistributed" fails because the meadows held as many elk as ever and the collared cows kept to their old ranges. "Rattled" fails because the filmed elk grazed heads down as long as before the wolves came.

P21.explanation: "Dried" fits: the ivy's overlapping leaves cover the wall like shingles, and the stone behind them held a third of the moisture of the bare stone, which soaks up rain, so the ivy kept the wall dry. "Fortified" fails because both halves stood firm in sound mortar and both survived the gale, so the ivy added no strength the wall lacked. "Dislodged" fails because stones on the ivy half stood as firm as on the bare half. "Etched" fails because the stone faces under the stems were clean.

P22.explanation: The ants lived in the thorns and drank the nectar, and shrubs freed of them flowered as heavily and grew a third taller, so the ants "parasitized" the shrub: they lived off it at a cost and gave nothing back. "Patrolled" fails because the ants were inside the thorns while the caterpillars fed in daylight, and banded and unbanded shrubs were chewed alike. "Pollinated" fails because banded shrubs flowered and podded as heavily without ants. "Propagated" fails because the seeds of shrubs with ants dropped beneath them just as the banded shrubs' did.

P23.explanation: The dune crept a few dozen yards a decade into the western gardens, and the families there gave up their houses one at a time as it reached them, so the sand had "nibbled" the village, taking it away in small pieces from one edge. "Lifted" fails because the families did not build upward over the sand; they moved a lane east and rebuilt on the same level ground. "Imprisoned" fails because caravans kept reaching the eastern gate throughout, so the village was never cut off. "Lashed" fails because the sand arrived as a slowly creeping dune that buried what it reached, not as sand flung against the walls.

P24.explanation: "Commandeered" fits: over the trustees' objections, the council filled the nave with flood victims' furniture and the town's emergency grain for three years, so it seized the church for public use. "Condemned" fails because engineers found the walls sound and the tower true, and the town used the building heavily. "Bulldozed" fails because the trustees got the church back in 1955. "Crated" fails because the church came back unaltered on its old site, so it was never taken apart and shipped away.

P25.explanation: The book matches the notebooks line by line except where the mother cursed her husband or wrote of leaving him, and there it substitutes mild phrases, so the daughter toned down the harsh passages: she "softened" the diary. "Tightened" means made more concise, but the book keeps even the weekly egg tallies, the first thing an editor cutting for length would drop. "Tidied" means cleaned up the writing, but the misspellings were printed as written. "Spliced" means joined in material from elsewhere, but nothing in the book comes from outside the notebooks.

P26.explanation: The drownings end in rescues and the child who starves survives on a neighbor's flour, so the translator "lightened" the novel, softening its darkness. "Mutilated" fails because he kept every chapter in order and changed only a few lines in a handful of scenes, so the book is whole, its grief eased rather than its body cut. "Naturalized" fails because he kept the family's names, its fjord and its money. "Manicured" fails because his sentences follow the original's short, abrupt rhythm clause by clause.

P27.explanation: "Dismantled" fits: the cargo lies spread along the storms' track, and the ship's own planks turn up all along that same line, so the winters have broken the hull apart and carried it off piece by piece. "Entombed" fails because the pieces lie on open sand and are rolled along the bottom each winter, never buried and sealed. "Encrusted" fails because that rolling scoured the planks smooth and pale, leaving nothing to crust on them. "Gnawed" fails because the planks' wood was still heavy and sound; the ship was broken up, not eaten into.

P28.explanation: Another printer reproduced her poems word for word, sold them at half her price in her own shops, and paid her nothing, so her poems had been "pirated": copied and sold without her share. "Plagiarized" fails because his edition carried her name on the title page, so no one passed the poems off as his own. "Panned" fails because the city papers had named two of the poems among the season's best. "Popularized" fails because the two editions together came to barely four hundred copies, so the poems reached hardly more readers than her own edition would have; the copies took her buyers rather than finding new ones.

P29.explanation: Doctors sent coughing townspeople up for the dry air, they stayed for months, and most went home well, so the monastery was where the valley's sick went to recover: a "sanatorium." A "tavern" serves passing travelers food and drink for pay, but guests came only with a doctor's letter and drovers on the road were sent on to the village inn. A "scriptorium" is where books are copied, but the monks bought even their prayer books from a printer. A "vault" keeps valuables safe, but what the books record it holding is guests paying monthly board, not anyone's wealth in safekeeping.

P30.explanation: "Cupboard" fits: the same few sharks returned every few weeks for six years, each taking a little and leaving the rest for later, so the carcass was a store of food they drew on over time. "Banquet" fails because there was no crowd and no single feast; a few sharks took a mouthful or two at a time. "Battery" fails because nothing lived on the carcass for it to sustain; it was simply flesh that visitors took away bit by bit. "Bridge" fails because the same few sharks came back to it rather than using it to pass anywhere.

P31.explanation: "Becalmed" fits: for nine days the ships stayed by the same headland with their canvas hanging and scraps floating beside them all day, so they had no wind to move them. "Blinded" fails because the ships stayed within sight of one another and of the headland, so they could see perfectly well. "Beached" fails because they lay off the headland on open water and then sailed on, so they were never ashore. "Capsized" fails because all five reached harbor without a spar broken.

P32.explanation: "Boycotted" fits: the wool was still being shipped from the port, and neutral buyers took more of it than ever, yet it vanished from the alliance's markets, so the alliance had stopped buying from the port. "Blockaded" fails because freighters bound for neutral countries still loaded wool at the port and no alliance warship came near the harbor. "Bombarded" fails because the waterfront sheds stood as before. "Annexed" fails because the island's flag still flew over the customs house.

P33.explanation: Water standing on dense clay could only evaporate, and the field could not carry a tractor until midsummer, so the flood had "mired" it, leaving it waterlogged and unworkable for weeks. "Leached" fails because the water sat on the clay rather than passing down through it, and the top foot of soil kept all its nitrogen. "Manured" fails because that unchanged nitrogen shows the flood added nothing to feed a crop. "Mulched" fails because the water ran clear from a reservoir and so brought no litter, and the clay's surface baked into cracked plates, which ground under a protective layer does not do.

P34.explanation: "Doctored" fits: the print copies the survey exactly everywhere except at the navy's harbor, where the safe channel has been moved onto a reef and false shoals block the real one, on a chart sold to foreign captains, so the engraver falsified the survey at the one place where misleading other navies mattered. "Flipped" fails because north is at the top of both and every other cape and bay matches the survey, so nothing was reversed. "Enlarged" fails because the print is the survey's size. "Gilded" fails because the print's open sea is as bare of ornament as the survey's; the only things added are false shoals, which change the chart's facts rather than dress it up.

P35.explanation: At the stop sign, where loaded trucks braked hard, the softened asphalt was shoved forward into folds crossing both lanes a stride apart, so the surface had been "rippled": raised into a series of small waves across the road. "Rutted" fails because on the climb, where trucks crawled in the same wheel tracks and grooves would form, the asphalt stayed level. "Raised" fails because the stakes showed the roadbed still at its laid height; the folds are in the asphalt, not a lift of the road. "Ruptured" fails because the asphalt nowhere cracked.

P36.explanation: The glacier's front advanced in every cold decade and retreated in every warm one, so its position tracked the climate, and the village records of where it lay register the temperature: it is the valley's "thermometer." A "storeroom" holds supplies for later use, but in dry summers the river runs as low as the rain-fed streams, so the glacier saves no water for the villages' dry months. A "timepiece" marks the hours, but with most meltwater sinking into gravel the river hardly changes from morning to night. A "signpost" points travelers along a route, but the only road over the mountains leaves the valley at its lower end, miles below the ice, so walking toward the glacier leads away from it.

P37.explanation: "Clinic" fits: fish hang still while the outcrop's shrimp feed on them, and where the shrimp are gone groupers carry three times the parasites, so the shrimp are eating the visitors' parasites; the outcrop is where reef fish go to be cleaned. "Canteen" fails because the feeding is done by the shrimp that live there, while the visiting fish hang motionless and eat nothing. "Bedroom" fails because the visits are by day and last minutes. "Ballroom" fails because the fish come singly and of mixed kinds, with no gathering of one species to court or spawn.

P38.explanation: "Corralled" fits: walking in a wide arc, the wolves pushed the elk ahead of them into a canyon of chest-deep drifts, a confined place where they could not escape. "Chased" fails because the wolves walked slowly and the elk moved off ahead of them, so the kills came from where the elk were pushed, not from outrunning them. "Ambushed" fails because the wolves came at the herd in the open, spread across the benches in plain sight, instead of waiting hidden. "Cowed" fails because by spring the elk were back on the benches and in the creek willows, so the pack did not frighten them out of their range.

P39.explanation: The single-ship channel made arriving ships cross one behind another, and the watchman on the point logged each one by name and hour, so the bar admitted and counted ships one at a time: a "turnstile." A "tollbooth" is where passing traffic pays, but the ships paid their duties later, at the customs house by the piers, so the payment point was there and the watchman at the bar only recorded them. A "wharf" is where cargo is handled, but ships unloaded at the piers after crossing. A "seawall" shelters a harbor, but winter swells rolled over the bar and broke against the piers.

P40.explanation: The officers crated and listed every piece, held the crates under guard, and sent the council the list with a sum beneath the total; once the sum was paid, the crates went back to the museum unopened, so the army had "ransomed" the collection. "Ransacked" fails because the pieces were crated, numbered and returned with their seals unbroken, the opposite of being rifled and scattered. "Requisitioned" fails because the army never put the pieces to any use: the crates sat under guard and went back once the city paid. "Repatriated" fails because the crates went back to the museum, not to the neighboring towns the pieces had come from.
